name: Agag king of the Amalekites
charge: The sword that made women childless
summary: The Lord had sworn war with Amalek from generation to generation for what they did to Israel on the way out of Egypt. Saul was sent to finish it and spared Agag. Samuel did not: as thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women.
offense: The command against Amalek reached back to its assault upon Israel in the wilderness. Amalek struck the hindmost, the feeble, and the weary, without fear of God; Israel was commanded to remember and blot out that memory when the Lord gave rest (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Exodus 17:14-16 placed the matter before succeeding generations. The passage of time had not discharged the word.
judgment: Samuel said, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites, and hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal. The sentence pronounced at Rephidim was carried out by a prophet's hand when the king's hand failed.

entries.commentary: At Rephidim there was no water, and the people did chide with Moses: wherefore is this that thou hast brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our cattle with thirst? At the first sign of trial the people jumped off the Lord's bandwagon again, the same as we do today when tribulation comes. Moses cried unto the Lord, What shall I do unto this people? they be almost ready to stone me. They were ready to kill the prophet over water, blaming the brother for what only the Most High controls; we have to build our faith up like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who trusted the Lord even when trials came.

The Lord stood before Moses upon the rock in Horeb; Moses smote the rock, and water came out of it in the sight of the elders of Israel. He called the place Massah and Meribah, temptation and chiding, because they tempted the Lord, saying, Is the Lord among us, or not? That is wickedness: He had just made Egypt dark, slain their firstborn, and sent His angel in the chariot to guide us, and the people still asked whether He was with them. The mercy of the Most High in bearing that is beyond us.

Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim. Amalek was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt; Amalek was Esau's grandson, born to Eliphaz of Timna the concubine, a duke in the land of Edom. When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed; when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed. Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands until the going down of the sun. Moses was about eighty years old holding a rod above his head all day; the fathers were mighty men, stronger than we are today. The sign shewed the people whose hand their life was in: Moses is the man to hearken to, so do not speak against him. And Joshua discomfited Amalek with the edge of the sword; Joshua was a mighty warrior even then.

Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven. Moses wrote it, and [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25) is that rehearsal: remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way. Amalek smote the hindmost, all that were feeble, when Israel was faint and weary, and he feared not God. He did not meet the mighty men in the front; he went to the back to slay the women, the children, and the old ones. That same spirit works against the nation's young and old today. The Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation. By the time Moses rehearsed it in Deuteronomy, forty years had passed and the children of Amalek had done nothing themselves; hundreds of years after that the Lord sent Saul by Samuel to smite Amalek for what was done coming out of Egypt. God be true and every man a liar: the nations do not get away with what they did to His people, and the judgment carries to the seed. Saul did not finish Agag's line, and in Esther's day Haman the Agagite of that same seed rose against Israel; the war truly runs from generation to generation. Today that seed says they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan, robbing Israel of identity and prospering off the oppression. The Lord says He will make them come and worship before thy feet, and to know that I have loved thee. The whole world is set up between Jacob and Esau, and Esau is the end of this world, the so-called white man, with Amalek leading; it is not speaking of the Arab man, for if Ishmael had a rulership still to come, Israel would have another captivity to enter, and Christ has already redeemed us from the curse of the law. The enmity was set from the garden between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed. They bruised Christ's heel, but at the end of the world Jacob bruises the head: the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly.

If there be a controversy between men, the judges justify the righteous and condemn the wicked; the wicked man worthy to be beaten was made to lie down and be beaten before the judge's face, according to his fault, by a certain number. Forty stripes may he give him, and not exceed, lest thy brother should seem vile unto thee. Paul recounted receiving that beating under this law.

Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn: the corn is the reward for the ox. Paul applies this verse to how the elders are treated: let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine, for the labourer is worthy of his reward. Giving double honour is not just saying the words to the leadership; it is true respect and reverence toward the leadership that labours in this word and doctrine.

If brethren dwell together and one of them die and have no child, the wife of the dead was not to marry without unto a stranger; her husband's brother took her to wife, and the firstborn she bare succeeded in the name of the dead brother, that his name be not put out of Israel. Check this out: this is no longer the law, so do not try to use it as an excuse toward your brother's wife. It stood for the name not being put out because of the land inheritance in Israel. The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother's wife loosed his shoe from off his foot, spat in his face, and answered, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house; and his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt: he met thee by the way and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary, and he feared not God. Israel was later commanded through Samuel to repay it: I remember that which Amalek did to Israel; now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not. At Rephidim, where Amalek first came and fought with Israel, the Lord told Moses to write this for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, for the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation; and that war is still going on even to this day.

Samuel said unto Saul, The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king over his people; now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the Lord. Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way when he came up from Egypt. Generations after the wilderness, the Most High still remembers; the generation of Amalekites had returned, and it was time to fulfil what was written. Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass. This is a specific instruction: kill all of them, spare none. Note that the Most High commanded this against a generation that had not personally done the deed in the wilderness; that answers the argument, I never did anything to you, so why hold it against me? The Most High himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember; this is a righteous grudge, and it shows [Leviticus 19:18](/bible/leviticus/19#v18) applies to the children of thy people.

Saul gathered the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand footmen and ten thousand men of Judah, and laid wait in the valley. Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed. The Most High discriminates righteously: the people who showed Israel kindness were spared out of the judgment.

Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur, and utterly destroyed the people with the edge of the sword; but he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive. He halfway fulfilled the order, reasoning like the king might be valuable as a hostage, as if the Lord forgot that detail. But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them; but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly. They killed what looked like it deserved killing, so they could say they did some killing, and kept the healthy, good looking animals, telling themselves surely the Lord could not have meant these.

Then came the word of the Lord unto Samuel: It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king, for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments. Mark the language: Saul did most of what was said, yet the Lord counts it as turning back and not performing his commandments at all. For everybody who says, well, I did do this part, understand: whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given unto you. That is what the Most High is showing us in this story. And it grieved Samuel, and he cried unto the Lord all night. Pride had to be in operation for Saul to transgress on that level, and pride is where the throne is lost.

Samuel rose early to meet Saul, and it was told him that Saul came to Carmel and set him up a place, a monument to himself, and is gone down to Gilgal. When your transgression becomes the lesson, be thankful when the correction comes quietly and nobody knows your name; do not take the spirit of bitterness, because you deserved a lot more. Saul greets Samuel first with a cover: Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord. The first thing out of his mouth is a fabrication, knowing full well he transgressed. Samuel answers, What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear? If you performed the commandment, why do I hear animals? Saul deflects again, the same blame game as chapter 13: They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed. Verse 9 already told us Saul and the people spared them; now suddenly it is only the people, and for a good reason, a sacrifice, as though the Lord ought to be pleased.

Samuel said, Stay, and I will tell thee what the Lord hath said to me this night. When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel? Samuel brings Saul back to his remembrance: when you thought nothing of yourself, with no confidence to be a ruler, the Most High still chose you. And the Lord sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed; the errand was the vengeance written in [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25). Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord? Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.

Saul is in denial: Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites. Samuel breaks down the rebuke and Saul tells the prophet he is wrong. In justifying himself over the animals, Saul volunteers even more of his rebellion, boasting that he spared the king, as if that was the smart move everyone really wanted; then he lays the spoil on the people again: the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.

Samuel makes it plain: Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. Do you think the Lord prefers a sacrifice to atone for broken commandments over you simply keeping the commandments? That is a heavy verse.

For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. That is heavy. A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this, and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway; according to this verse, that rebellion is the same as witchcraft. Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction does not come from the man; it is the commandment of the Lord that leadership carries. When you are stubborn against it, you are saying what I want to do comes before what God wants me to do, and you have put yourself in the midst of idolatry as surely as circling the stone at Mecca or bowing before a cross. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king: you will lose whatever position the Most High put you in. This stubborn heart is what fares evil at the last; we will read Saul's end in the last chapter of 1 Samuel, and in chapter 16 the evil spirit enters into him and the Spirit of the Lord departs. The plant of wickedness took root here.

Now the confession finally comes, and it is still not sincere: I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord and thy words; because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. Even in admitting it he deflects: it is the fault of the wicked people you put me over. Then he asks, Pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord; take me back to the regular Saul and Samuel connection, as though a fearful excuse settles it.

Samuel refuses: I will not return with thee; for thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath rejected thee from being king over Israel. Think it through: Samuel gave Saul the opening at the bleating of the sheep, and Saul would not humble down; he asked why Saul disobeyed the voice of the Lord, and Saul justified himself again. Two admonitions were given and refused before this rejection.

As Samuel turned about to go away, Saul laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent. And Samuel said, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou. Just as Saul tore the hem of the garment, so the Lord tore the throne from him; and Samuel says this still before he has ever met David, the same word he gave in chapter 13. And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent. The Strength of Israel is the Most High. Understand the spirit of the title: whenever you go off on your own mind, pride has you departing from your strength, and once you have left your strength you are open to Satan; if a brother tells you that you are battling with pride, take heed and examine yourself.

Then he said, I have sinned: yet honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel. This spirit is very real: okay, you are right, but do not let the people see the demotion; make sure they still know I am the king. That is the spirit of vanity, caught up in a rank and a title while forgetting that the title came for pleasing the Lord; once you discontinue pleasing the Lord, the title is going to leave as well. So Samuel turned again after Saul, and Saul worshipped the Lord.

Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately, and said, Surely the bitterness of death is past; with Saul under rebuke, Agag figured nobody was mad at the Amalekites anymore and he was safe. And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal. The old prophet did not play; he finished the commandment himself, measure for measure for what Amalek's sword had done.

Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah, and Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul, and the Lord repented that he had made Saul king over Israel. The mourning is what makes it sad: Samuel raised Saul up from nothing, saw his potential, and saw the Spirit come upon him in chapter 11 when he stood up as a savior for the people; he had hope in him, and it came to this. Samuel was grieved, and the Lord repented of the appointment. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

verses.text: And the Lord said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.
And Moses built an altar, and called the name of it JEHOVAH–nissi:
For he said, Because the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt;
How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.

Therefore it shall be, when the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.
Samuel also said unto Saul, The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king over his people, over Israel: now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the Lord.
Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.
And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword.

But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.
Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately. And Agag said, Surely the bitterness of death is past.
And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal.
